title: Κλῆρος καὶ Κίρκης δώματα
titleEn: The Lot and Circe’s Hall — Odyssey 10.174–273
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his tale, rouses his companions from their grief after the stag: they will not go down to Hades before their day, so let them eat. They feast until dark, and at dawn he calls an assembly and says that he has climbed a lookout and seen an island, low and wooded, with smoke rising from its middle. The men break down, remembering Antiphates and the Cyclops. He divides them into two bands, himself leading one and Eurylochus the other, and the lot to go falls to Eurylochus and twenty-two men. They find Circe’s hall in a glen, ringed by wolves and lions that she has bewitched, which fawn on them like dogs on a master. Polites calls out, Circe opens the shining doors, and all but Eurylochus follow. She gives them a drugged mixture and strikes them with a wand, and they are penned in the sties with the heads, voices and bristles of swine but their own minds. Eurylochus comes back to the ship, unable at first to speak, and tells what he saw. Odysseus takes sword and bow and orders him to lead the way back, but Eurylochus clasps his knees, begs not to be taken there, and urges flight. Odysseus tells him to stay by the ship and eat and drink, and says he will go himself, since necessity is upon him.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γάρ πω καταδυσόμεθ’ ἀχνύμενοί περ
εἰς Ἀίδαο δόμους, πρὶν μόρσιμον ἦμαρ ἐπέλθῃ·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, ou gar pō katadysometh’ achnymenoi per
eis Aidao domous, prin morsimon ēmar epelthēi·
sentences.l:
‘O friends, for not yet shall we go down, grieving though we are,
to the halls of Hades, before the allotted day comes upon us;
sentences.i: ‘Friends, we shall not yet go down to the halls of Hades, grieving though we are, before our allotted day comes upon us;
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is 'O friends', Odysseus speaking to the crew; the single quotes are because the whole tale is itself Odysseus's speech at the Phaeacian court. οὐ γάρ πω is 'for not yet', and γάρ gives his reason for courage. καταδυσόμεθ’ is the future of καταδύω 'go down', and ἀχνύμενοί περ is 'grieving though we are'. Ἀίδαο is the epic genitive of Ἅιδης (-αο for -ου), and εἰς … δόμους 'to the halls' is the stock way to say the dwelling of the dead. πρίν with the subjunctive ἐπέλθῃ is 'before it comes upon (us)', and μόρσιμον ἦμαρ is 'the allotted day', from μόρος 'portion, fate'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’, ὄφρ’ ἐν νηὶ θοῇ βρῶσίς τε πόσις τε,
μνησόμεθα βρώμης, μηδὲ τρυχώμεθα λιμῷ.
sentences.tr:
all’ aget’, ophr’ en nēi thoēi brōsis te posis te,
mnēsometha brōmēs, mēde trychōmetha limōi.
sentences.l:
But come, while in the swift ship there is both food and drink,
let us think of eating, and let us not be worn down by hunger.’
sentences.i: But come, while there is food and drink in the swift ship, let us think of eating, and not be worn down by hunger.’
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ is 'but come', the plural of ἀλλ’ ἄγε. ὄφρα is 'while', here with no verb: 'while there is food and drink'. νηὶ θοῇ is 'swift ship'. μνησόμεθα is a short-vowel subjunctive (= μνησώμεθα) of μιμνήσκομαι 'remember, be mindful of', with the genitive βρώμης 'of eating', used as an exhortation, 'let us think of'. μηδὲ τρυχώμεθα is 'and let us not be worn down', a present subjunctive of τρύχω 'wear out', with the dative λιμῷ 'by hunger'. The unit closes the speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, οἱ δ’ ὦκα ἐμοῖς ἐπέεσσι πίθοντο,
ἐκ δὲ καλυψάμενοι παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο
θηήσαντ’ ἔλαφον·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, hoi d’ ōka emois epeessi pithonto,
ek de kalypsamenoi para thin’ halos atrygetoio
thēēsant’ elaphon·
sentences.i: So I spoke, and they quickly yielded to my words; they uncovered themselves, and along the shore of the sea that yields no harvest they gazed at the stag;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is 'so I spoke', ἐφάμην being the first person of the imperfect of φημί. πίθοντο is a strong aorist of πείθομαι 'be persuaded, obey' with no augment, and ἐπέεσσι is the dative plural 'with/to words'. ἐκ … καλυψάμενοι is tmesis for the participle of ἐκκαλύπτομαι 'uncover oneself': the object is not stated, and the likeliest sense is that the men had wrapped themselves up in their grief. θῖν’ is θῖνα, accusative of θίς 'shore, beach'. ἁλὸς ἀτρυγέτοιο is the stock phrase 'of the unharvested salt-sea'; the meaning of ἀτρύγετος is not known, 'unharvested' being only the old guess. θηήσαντ’ is the aorist of θηέομαι 'gaze at', again without augment.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ μέγα θηρίον ἦεν.
sentences.tr: mala gar mega thērion ēen.
sentences.l: for very great a beast it was.
sentences.i: for it was a very big beast.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason they stared. θηρίον is 'wild animal, beast', here the stag, and μάλα … μέγα is 'very great'; ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί. This is the same line as 10.171 and has the same English.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάρπησαν ὁρώμενοι ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
χεῖρας νιψάμενοι τεύχοντ’ ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα.
sentences.tr:
autar epei tarpēsan horōmenoi ophthalmoisin,
cheiras nipsamenoi teuchont’ erikydea daita.
sentences.l:
But when they had had their fill, looking with their eyes,
hands having washed, they prepared a glorious feast.
sentences.i: But when they had feasted their eyes to the full, they washed their hands and prepared a glorious feast.
sentences.n: The first line is the same as elsewhere in the poem and keeps its English. τάρπησαν is the aorist passive of τέρπω 'satisfy', so τάρπησαν ὁρώμενοι ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is 'they were satisfied by looking with their eyes', that is they had their fill of the sight. χεῖρας νιψάμενοι is 'having washed their hands', and τεύχοντ’ is the middle imperfect of τεύχω 'make ready'. ἐρικυδέα δαῖτα is 'a glorious feast', the epithet from κῦδος 'glory'.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
ἥμεθα δαινύμενοι κρέα τ’ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
hōs tote men propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
hēmetha dainymenoi krea t’ aspeta kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.n: The same two lines as elsewhere in the poem, with the same English. πρόπαν ἦμαρ is 'the whole day', the accusative of duration, and ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα 'until the sun going down'. ἥμεθα is 'we sat', and δαινύμενοι is 'feasting'. ἄσπετα is 'boundless', literally 'not to be told', and μέθυ ἡδύ is 'sweet wine'. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθε,
δὴ τότε κοιμήθημεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ēelios katedy kai epi knephas ēlthe,
dē tote koimēthēmen epi rhēgmini thalassēs.
sentences.l:
And when the sun set and darkness came on,
then indeed we lay down to sleep upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: And when the sun set and darkness came on, then we lay down to sleep on the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: The same two lines as elsewhere in the poem, with the same English. ἦμος is 'when', and the aorists κατέδυ 'set' and ἦλθε 'came' are ordinary past tenses. κνέφας is 'darkness'. κοιμήθημεν is the aorist passive of κοιμάω, 'we were put to sleep', that is 'lay down to sleep'. ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης is 'on the surf-line of the sea', the place where the waves break.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἀγορὴν θέμενος μετὰ πᾶσιν ἔειπον·
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ ērigeneia phanē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
kai tot’ egōn agorēn themenos meta pasin eeipon·
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
then I, an assembly having set, among all spoke:
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, I called an assembly and spoke among them all:
sentences.n: The dawn line comes again with the same English. ἠριγένεια is 'early-born' and ῥοδοδάκτυλος 'rose-fingered', both fixed epithets of Dawn. The main clause is καὶ τότ’ 'and then', with ἐγών the epic form of ἐγώ 'I'. ἀγορὴν θέμενος is 'having set an assembly', that is 'having called a meeting', and μετὰ πᾶσιν ἔειπον is 'I spoke among them all', ἔειπον being an aorist. The ano teleia and the next unit's quotation mark show that a speech follows.

sentences.t: κέκλυτέ μευ μύθων, κακά περ πάσχοντες ἑταῖροι·
sentences.tr: keklyte meu mythōn, kaka per paschontes hetairoi·
sentences.l: ‘Hear my words, evils though suffering, companions;
sentences.i: ‘Hear my words, companions, suffering woes as you are;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear', used as a call for attention, and μευ is the genitive 'of me', here 'my', going with μύθων 'words'. κακά περ πάσχοντες is 'though suffering evils', περ giving the concession, and ἑταῖροι is the vocative 'companions'. This opens the speech Odysseus gives at the assembly; the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γάρ τ’ ἴδμεν, ὅπῃ ζόφος οὐδ’ ὅπῃ ἠώς,
οὐδ’ ὅπῃ ἠέλιος φαεσίμβροτος εἶσ’ ὑπὸ γαῖαν,
οὐδ’ ὅπῃ ἀννεῖται·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, ou gar t’ idmen, hopēi zophos oud’ hopēi ēōs,
oud’ hopēi ēelios phaesimbrotos eis’ hypo gaian,
oud’ hopēi anneitai·
sentences.i: Friends, for we do not know where the darkness lies or where the dawn, nor where the sun, who gives light to mortals, goes beneath the earth, nor where it rises again;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ τ’ ἴδμεν is 'for we do not know', ἴδμεν being the epic form of ἴσμεν, 'we know', and τε here is the epic particle of general statement. ὅπῃ is 'where, in which direction', and comes four times in the unit, the last three as οὐδ’ ὅπῃ. ζόφος is 'gloom, the dark quarter' and ἠώς 'dawn'; they stand for west and east. φαεσίμβροτος is 'giving light to mortals', and εἶσ’ is εἶσι 'goes'. ἀννεῖται is the contracted ἀνανέεται, 'comes up again', the verb of the sun's return.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ φραζώμεθα θᾶσσον
εἴ τις ἔτ’ ἔσται μῆτις.
sentences.tr:
alla phrazōmetha thasson
ei tis et’ estai mētis.
sentences.l:
but let us consider more quickly
whether there will still be any cunning.
sentences.i: but let us consider quickly whether any cunning is left to us.
sentences.n: φραζώμεθα is the subjunctive of φράζομαι 'consider, plan', used as an exhortation, and θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, 'more quickly' (the second layer says simply 'quickly'). εἰ is 'whether'. μῆτις is 'cunning intelligence, craft', the word behind πολύμητις; it is not μηχανή 'device'. ἔσται is the future 'there will be'. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 193.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δ’ οὐκ οἴομαι εἶναι.
sentences.tr: egō d’ ouk oiomai einai.
sentences.l: but I do not think there is.
sentences.i: though I do not think there is any.
sentences.n: οἴομαι 'I think' is the contracted form of ὀΐομαι, with the infinitive εἶναι giving 'I do not think it exists'. The whole line has a full stop in its middle, and what comes before has just raised the question, so this short unit is the answer to it.

sentences.t:
εἶδον γὰρ σκοπιὴν ἐς παιπαλόεσσαν ἀνελθὼν
νῆσον, τὴν πέρι πόντος ἀπείριτος ἐστεφάνωται·
sentences.tr:
eidon gar skopiēn es paipaloessan anelthōn
nēson, tēn peri pontos apeiritos estephanōtai·
sentences.l:
For I saw, to a rugged lookout having gone up,
an island, which round the limitless open-sea is wreathed;
sentences.i: for I climbed to a rugged lookout and saw an island, round which the limitless sea lies like a wreath;
sentences.n: εἶδον is the aorist 'I saw'. σκοπιὴν ἐς παιπαλόεσσαν ἀνελθών is 'having gone up to a rugged lookout', σκοπιή being 'watch-place' and παιπαλόεσσαν 'rugged'. The relative τὴν πέρι is 'around which', with the preposition placed after the pronoun it governs. ἀπείριτος is 'limitless' and ἐστεφάνωται, perfect passive of στεφανόω, is 'is wreathed', 'is crowned': the sea lies round the island as a garland lies round a head.

sentences.t: αὐτὴ δὲ χθαμαλὴ κεῖται·
sentences.tr: autē de chthamalē keitai·
sentences.l: and itself low it lies;
sentences.i: and the island itself lies low;
sentences.n: αὐτή is 'itself', the island. χθαμαλή is 'low, close to the ground', and κεῖται is 'lies'. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 196.

sentences.t:
καπνὸν δ’ ἐνὶ μέσσῃ
ἔδρακον ὀφθαλμοῖσι διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλην.
sentences.tr:
kapnon d’ eni messēi
edrakon ophthalmoisi dia dryma pykna kai hylēn.
sentences.l:
and smoke in the middle
I saw with my eyes, through thick coppices and woodland.’
sentences.i: and in the middle of it I saw smoke with my eyes, through thick coppices and woodland.’
sentences.n: καπνὸν … ἔδρακον is 'I saw smoke', ἔδρακον being the aorist of δέρκομαι 'see'. ἐνὶ μέσσῃ is 'in the middle', the feminine standing for the middle of the island. διά with the accusative is 'through', and δρυμά is 'coppices', a neuter plural, with ὕλην 'woodland'; the half-line διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλην is the same as at 10.148 and has the same English. The unit closes Odysseus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, τοῖσιν δὲ κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ
μνησαμένοις ἔργων Λαιστρυγόνος Ἀντιφάταο
Κύκλωπός τε βίης μεγαλήτορος, ἀνδροφάγοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn, toisin de kateklasthē philon ētor
mnēsamenois ergōn Laistrygonos Antiphatao
Kyklōpos te biēs megalētoros, androphagoio.
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and in them was broken their dear heart,
as they remembered the deeds of Antiphates the Laestrygonian
and the Cyclops’ great-spirited might, man-eating.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and their dear hearts were broken within them as they remembered the deeds of Antiphates the Laestrygonian and the great-spirited might of the Cyclops, that eater of men.
sentences.n: τοῖσιν is the epic dative 'in them' or 'to them', with φίλον ἦτορ 'dear heart', the singular standing for the heart of each man. κατεκλάσθη is the aorist passive of κατακλάω 'break down'. μνησαμένοις is the dative plural participle 'to those remembering', with the genitives ἔργων 'the deeds' and, in the next lines, βίης 'the might'. Λαιστρυγόνος Ἀντιφάταο is 'Antiphates the Laestrygonian', with the epic genitive -αο. μεγαλήτορος can agree either with βίης or with Κύκλωπος; μεγαλήτωρ is kept 'great-spirited'. ἀνδροφάγοιο is 'man-eating', from ἀνήρ and φαγεῖν, and agrees with the Cyclops.

sentences.t: κλαῖον δὲ λιγέως θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες·
sentences.tr: klaion de ligeōs thaleron kata dakry cheontes·
sentences.l: and they wept clearly, an abundant tear shedding;
sentences.i: and they wept with clear voices, shedding abundant tears;
sentences.n: κλαῖον is the imperfect of κλαίω 'weep'. λιγέως is the adverb of λιγύς 'clear-sounding', the first part of λιγύφθογγοι in the fixed 'clear-voiced heralds': the weeping rings out. θαλερὸν δάκρυ is 'abundant tear', θαλερός 'abundant, flourishing'. κατὰ … χέοντες is tmesis for 'pouring down', so 'shedding'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ τις πρῆξις ἐγίγνετο μυρομένοισιν.
sentences.tr: all’ ou gar tis prēxis egigneto myromenoisin.
sentences.l: but not any accomplishing came about for them lamenting.
sentences.i: but nothing was accomplished by their lamenting.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ γάρ is 'but (it did no good), for …'; the thought the Greek leaves out is that weeping was useless. πρῆξις is 'a doing, an accomplishing, result', and ἐγίγνετο 'came about'. μυρομένοισιν is the dative plural participle of μύρομαι 'lament', 'to/for them lamenting'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ δίχα πάντας ἐυκνήμιδας ἑταίρους
ἠρίθμεον, ἀρχὸν δὲ μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ὄπασσα·
sentences.tr:
autar egō dicha pantas eyknēmidas hetairous
ērithmeon, archon de met’ amphoteroisin opassa·
sentences.l:
But I, in two, all my well-greaved companions
counted, and a leader to each of the two I gave;
sentences.i: But I divided all my well-greaved companions into two groups, counting them off, and gave each group a leader;
sentences.n: δίχα is 'in two parts'. ἐυκνήμιδας ἑταίρους is 'well-greaved companions', the greaves being shin-guards, and it is a stock epithet. ἠρίθμεον is the uncontracted imperfect of ἀριθμέω 'count'. ἀρχόν is 'a leader', and ὄπασσα is the aorist of ὀπάζω 'grant, give'. μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν is 'among both (groups)'.

sentences.t: τῶν μὲν ἐγὼν ἦρχον, τῶν δ’ Εὐρύλοχος θεοειδής.
sentences.tr: tōn men egōn ērchon, tōn d’ Eurylochos theoeidēs.
sentences.l: of the one I was the leader, of the other Eurylochus, godlike-in-form.
sentences.i: I led the one, and Eurylochus, godlike in form, the other.
sentences.n: τῶν μέν … τῶν δέ is 'of these … of those', each article standing for a group, and ἄρχω takes the genitive, so ἦρχον is 'I led'. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. Εὐρύλοχος is named here for the first time in this part. θεοειδής is 'godlike in form' (θεός and εἶδος).

sentences.t: κλήρους δ’ ἐν κυνέῃ χαλκήρεϊ πάλλομεν ὦκα·
sentences.tr: klērous d’ en kyneēi chalkēreï pallomen ōka·
sentences.l: and lots in a helmet, bronze-fitted, we shook quickly;
sentences.i: and we quickly shook lots in a bronze-fitted helmet;
sentences.n: κλήρους are lots, here marked pieces thrown into a helmet and shaken. κυνέη is a helmet, originally a cap of dog-skin, and χαλκήρεϊ is the dative of χαλκήρης 'fitted with bronze'. πάλλομεν is 'we shook' and ὦκα 'quickly'.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἔθορε κλῆρος μεγαλήτορος Εὐρυλόχοιο.
sentences.tr: ek d’ ethore klēros megalētoros Eurylochoio.
sentences.l: and out leapt the lot of great-spirited Eurylochus.
sentences.i: and out leapt the lot of great-spirited Eurylochus.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἔθορε is 'leapt out', the aorist of θρῴσκω, and the lot that jumps out of a shaken helmet is the one chosen. μεγαλήτορος Εὐρυλόχοιο is the genitive with the epic ending -οιο, and μεγαλήτωρ is 'great-spirited'.

sentences.t:
βῆ δ’ ἰέναι, ἅμα τῷ γε δύω καὶ εἴκοσ’ ἑταῖροι
κλαίοντες·
sentences.tr:
bē d’ ienai, hama tōi ge dyō kai eikos’ hetairoi
klaiontes·
sentences.l:
and he set out to go, and along with him two and twenty companions,
weeping;
sentences.i: and he set out, and with him twenty-two companions, weeping;
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἰέναι is the formula 'and he set out to go', βῆ being the aorist of βαίνω without augment and ἰέναι the infinitive. ἅμα τῷ γε is 'together with him', the pronoun τῷ and the particle γε. δύω καὶ εἴκοσι is 'two and twenty', which with Eurylochus makes twenty-three men. κλαίοντες is 'weeping'. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 209.

sentences.t: κατὰ δ’ ἄμμε λίπον γοόωντας ὄπισθεν.
sentences.tr: kata d’ amme lipon gooōntas opisthen.
sentences.l: and us they left behind, lamenting, in the rear.
sentences.i: and they left us behind, mourning.
sentences.n: κατὰ … λίπον is tmesis for καταλείπω 'leave behind'. ἄμμε is the Aeolic accusative 'us' (Attic ἡμᾶς). γοόωντας is the uncontracted participle of γοάω 'groan, lament', and ὄπισθεν is 'behind'. The subject of λίπον is the party that went.

sentences.t:
εὗρον δ’ ἐν βήσσῃσι τετυγμένα δώματα Κίρκης
ξεστοῖσιν λάεσσι, περισκέπτῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ·
sentences.tr:
heuron d’ en bēssēisi tetygmena dōmata Kirkēs
xestoisin laessi, periskeptōi eni chōrōi·
sentences.l:
and they found in the glens the well-wrought halls of Circe
of smoothed stones, in a place with a view all round;
sentences.i: In the glens they found the well-wrought halls of Circe, built of smoothed stone, in a place with a view all around;
sentences.n: εὗρον is the aorist 'they found'. βήσσῃσι is the dative plural of βῆσσα 'glen, wooded valley'. τετυγμένα is the perfect passive participle of τεύχω, 'well-wrought', 'built'. ξεστοῖσιν λάεσσι is 'smoothed stones', ξεστός being 'scraped smooth', and λάεσσι is the dative plural of λᾶας 'stone'. περισκέπτῳ is 'to be seen all round', and may mean either that the place can be seen from all sides or that it commands a view; the English phrase 'with a view all round' is meant to keep both readings open, and the note does not decide. Line 211 comes again at 253.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν λύκοι ἦσαν ὀρέστεροι ἠδὲ λέοντες,
τοὺς αὐτὴ κατέθελξεν, ἐπεὶ κακὰ φάρμακ’ ἔδωκεν.
sentences.tr:
amphi de min lykoi ēsan oresteroi ēde leontes,
tous autē katethelxen, epei kaka pharmak’ edōken.
sentences.l:
and around it were wolves, of the mountains, and lions,
whom she herself had bewitched, since evil drugs she had given.
sentences.i: Around it were mountain wolves and lions, which she herself had bewitched by giving them evil drugs.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … μιν is 'around it', the house. ὀρέστεροι is 'of the mountains'. τοὺς is the relative 'whom' (the pronoun-article used as a relative), and αὐτή is 'she herself'. κατέθελξεν is the aorist of καταθέλγω 'charm, bewitch'. κακὰ φάρμακ’ is 'evil drugs', φάρμακον being any drug, for good or ill, and ἔδωκεν 'she gave'. The beasts are not described as men, only as bewitched.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ οἵ γ’ ὡρμήθησαν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν, ἀλλ’ ἄρα τοί γε
οὐρῇσιν μακρῇσι περισσαίνοντες ἀνέσταν.
sentences.tr:
oud’ hoi g’ hōrmēthēsan ep’ andrasin, all’ ara toi ge
ourēisin makrēisi perissainontes anestan.
sentences.l:
Nor did they rush upon the men, but, to be sure, they
with long tails fawning round rose up.
sentences.i: They did not rush at the men; instead they rose up around them, fawning with their long tails.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ οἵ γε is 'nor did they', the beasts, with οἵ as a pronoun. ὡρμήθησαν is the aorist passive of ὁρμάω 'rush, set upon' with ἐπί and the dative ἀνδράσιν. ἀλλ’ ἄρα τοί γε is 'but they, in fact'. οὐρῇσιν μακρῇσι is 'with long tails', the dative plural of οὐρή. περισσαίνοντες is 'fawning all round', and ἀνέσταν is the root aorist of ἀνίστημι, third plural in -αν (Attic ἀνέστησαν), 'rose up'.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα κύνες δαίτηθεν ἰόντα
σαίνωσ’, αἰεὶ γάρ τε φέρει μειλίγματα θυμοῦ,
ὣς τοὺς ἀμφὶ λύκοι κρατερώνυχες ἠδὲ λέοντες
σαῖνον·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an amphi anakta kynes daitēthen ionta
sainōs’, aiei gar te pherei meiligmata thymou,
hōs tous amphi lykoi kraterōnyches ēde leontes
sainon·
sentences.l:
As when around their lord, from the feast coming, dogs
fawn, for he always brings soothings of the heart,
so around them the wolves, strong-clawed, and lions
fawned;
sentences.i: As dogs fawn around their master when he comes from the feast, for he always brings something to soothe the heart, so the strong-clawed wolves and the lions fawned around them;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν … σαίνωσι is 'as when … fawn', the subjunctive giving a general case. ἄνακτα is 'lord', here the dogs' master, and δαίτηθεν is 'from the feast', the suffix -θεν marking the place from which. The τε in αἰεὶ γάρ τε is the epic particle of general truth. μειλίγματα θυμοῦ is 'things that soothe the heart', μείλιγμα being a means of soothing. ὣς τοὺς ἀμφί is 'so around them', with the preposition placed after the pronoun it governs. κρατερώνυχες is 'strong-clawed', from κρατερός and ὄνυξ, a word that can mean either 'claw' or 'hoof'; for wolves and lions it is the claw. σαῖνον is the imperfect 'fawned'. The comparison runs across four lines and ends at the ano teleia mid-line.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἔδεισαν, ἐπεὶ ἴδον αἰνὰ πέλωρα.
sentences.tr: toi d’ edeisan, epei idon aina pelōra.
sentences.l: and they were afraid, since they saw fearsome monsters.
sentences.i: and the men were afraid, for they saw fearsome monsters.
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ is 'and they', the men, with τοί as a pronoun. ἔδεισαν is the aorist of δείδω 'fear', and ἴδον is the aorist 'they saw', without augment. αἰνά is 'fearsome', and πέλωρα is the neuter plural of πέλωρ 'monster', 'huge creature'.

sentences.t:
ἔσταν δ’ ἐν προθύροισι θεᾶς καλλιπλοκάμοιο,
Κίρκης δ’ ἔνδον ἄκουον ἀειδούσης ὀπὶ καλῇ,
ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένης μέγαν ἄμβροτον, οἷα θεάων
λεπτά τε καὶ χαρίεντα καὶ ἀγλαὰ ἔργα πέλονται.
sentences.tr:
estan d’ en prothyroisi theas kalliplokamoio,
Kirkēs d’ endon akouon aeidousēs opi kalēi,
histon epoichomenēs megan ambroton, hoia theaōn
lepta te kai charienta kai aglaa erga pelontai.
sentences.l:
And they stood in the forecourt of the goddess fair-plaited,
and Circe within they heard singing with a beautiful voice,
as she went to and fro at a great loom, deathless, such as of goddesses
the delicate and graceful and splendid works are.
sentences.i: They stood in the forecourt of the fair-plaited goddess, and heard Circe inside, singing in a beautiful voice as she moved to and fro at a great, deathless loom, such as the works of goddesses are, delicate and graceful and splendid.
sentences.n: ἔσταν is the third plural of the root aorist ἔστην (Attic ἔστησαν), 'they stood', and προθύροισι is the dative plural of πρόθυρον 'forecourt'. θεᾶς καλλιπλοκάμοιο is 'of the goddess with fair plaits'; the goddess is not named until the next line, and Κίρκης is the genitive after ἄκουον, with the participle ἀειδούσης 'singing'. ἄκουον is 'they heard', ὀπὶ καλῇ 'with a beautiful voice', the same words and English as at 5.61. ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένης is 'going to and fro at the loom', ἱστός being both 'loom' and 'web'. ἄμβροτον is 'deathless' (an old word for what belongs to the gods). οἷα … πέλονται is 'such as … are', with the works of goddesses described by three adjectives, λεπτά 'delicate, fine-spun', χαρίεντα 'graceful', and ἀγλαά 'splendid'. The sentence runs four lines and ends at a full stop.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε Πολίτης ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν,
ὅς μοι κήδιστος ἑτάρων ἦν κεδνότατός τε·
sentences.tr:
toisi de mythōn ērche Politēs orchamos andrōn,
hos moi kēdistos hetarōn ēn kednotatos te·
sentences.l:
And among them of speeches made-beginning Polites, chief of men,
who to me of my companions was the closest-tied and the most trusty;
sentences.i: Polites, chief of men, was the first to speak among them, he who was the closest of my companions and the most trusty;
sentences.n: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε is the formula 'and he was the first to speak among them', with μύθων the genitive after ἄρχω. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν is 'chief of men'. The relative ὅς … ἦν is 'who was', and μοι the dative 'to me, for me'. κήδιστος is the superlative of a word from κῆδος 'care, tie', 'closest-tied', and κεδνότατος is the superlative of κεδνός 'trusty'; both take the genitive ἑτάρων 'of companions'. Here Odysseus the narrator says what Polites was to him; the next unit is Polites's speech.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, ἔνδον γάρ τις ἐποιχομένη μέγαν ἱστὸν
καλὸν ἀοιδιάει, δάπεδον δ’ ἅπαν ἀμφιμέμυκεν,
ἢ θεὸς ἠὲ γυνή·
sentences.tr:
ō philoi, endon gar tis epoichomenē megan histon
kalon aoidiaei, dapedon d’ hapan amphimemyken,
ē theos ēe gynē·
sentences.i: ‘Friends, for someone inside, moving to and fro at a great loom, is singing finely, and the whole floor echoes all around; either a goddess or a woman;
sentences.n: ἔνδον γάρ τις is 'for someone inside', with the sentence's verb held back to the next line. ἐποιχομένη μέγαν ἱστόν has the words of the previous unit's ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένης μέγαν, now in the feminine nominative and in a different order. ἀοιδιάει is 'sings', a verb built on ἀοιδή 'song' that does the work of ἀείδω. δάπεδον is 'floor', and ἀμφιμέμυκεν is the perfect of ἀμφιμυκάομαι 'echo, ring all round'. ἢ θεὸς ἠὲ γυνή is 'either goddess or woman', with the same word θεός used of a goddess.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ φθεγγώμεθα θᾶσσον.
sentences.tr: alla phthengōmetha thasson.
sentences.l: but let us call out more quickly.’
sentences.i: but let us call out quickly.’
sentences.n: φθεγγώμεθα is the subjunctive of φθέγγομαι 'utter a sound, call out', used as an exhortation, and θᾶσσον is 'more quickly' (the second layer says simply 'quickly'). The unit closes Polites's speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, τοὶ δὲ φθέγγοντο καλεῦντες.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephōnēsen, toi de phthengonto kaleuntes.
sentences.l: So then he called out, and they raised their voices, calling.
sentences.i: So he called out, and they raised their voices and called.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν is 'so then he called out', ἐφώνησεν being the aorist of φωνέω 'speak aloud'. τοὶ δέ is 'and they', and φθέγγοντο καλεῦντες is 'raised their voices, calling', the participle being καλεῦντες, a form of καλέοντες of καλέω 'call' with εο run together as ευ (Attic καλοῦντες). Nobody is named as the one called; the next lines show that Circe is meant.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αἶψ’ ἐξελθοῦσα θύρας ὤιξε φαεινὰς
καὶ κάλει·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ aips’ exelthousa thyras ōixe phaeinas
kai kalei·
sentences.l:
And she at once, coming out, opened the shining doors
and called;
sentences.i: She came out at once, opened the shining doors, and called to them;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is 'and she', the article used as a pronoun. ἐξελθοῦσα is the aorist participle 'having come out', and ὤιξε is the aorist of ἀνοίγνυμι 'open', with the augment worked into the stem. φαεινάς is 'shining'. κάλει is the imperfect of καλέω 'was calling'. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 231, and 256–257 repeat these lines.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἀιδρείῃσιν ἕποντο·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ hama pantes aidreiēisin heponto·
sentences.l: and they, all together, in their ignorance followed;
sentences.i: and in their ignorance they all followed together;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is 'and they', the men. ἀιδρείῃσιν is the dative plural of ἀιδρείη 'ignorance, lack of knowledge', 'in their ignorance', and ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow'. The next unit shows that one man did not.

sentences.t: Εὐρύλοχος δ’ ὑπέμεινεν, ὀισάμενος δόλον εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Eurylochos d’ hypemeinen, oisamenos dolon einai.
sentences.l: but Eurylochus stayed behind, suspecting that it was a trick.
sentences.i: but Eurylochus stayed behind, suspecting that it was a trick.
sentences.n: ὑπέμεινεν is the aorist of ὑπομένω 'stay behind, hold back'. ὀισάμενος is the aorist participle of ὀΐομαι 'suspect, think', and δόλον εἶναι is 'that it was a trick', with δόλος 'trick, deceit'.

sentences.t:
εἷσεν δ’ εἰσαγαγοῦσα κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε,
ἐν δέ σφιν τυρόν τε καὶ ἄλφιτα καὶ μέλι χλωρὸν
οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ ἐκύκα·
sentences.tr:
heisen d’ eisagagousa kata klismous te thronous te,
en de sphin tyron te kai alphita kai meli chlōron
oinōi Pramneiōi ekyka·
sentences.i: She led them in and seated them along the seats and the chairs, and stirred cheese and barley-meal and yellow honey into Pramnian wine for them;
sentences.n: εἷσεν is the aorist of ἵζω in its transitive sense, 'seated'. εἰσαγαγοῦσα is 'having led in'. κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε is 'along the seats and the chairs', as at 1.145 and 3.389: κλισμός is a chair with a back to lean on, and θρόνος a high chair, not a throne. ἐν … ἐκύκα is tmesis for 'stirred in', the imperfect of κυκάω 'stir, mix', and σφιν is 'for them'. ἄλφιτα is barley-meal and χλωρόν a pale greenish-yellow, 'yellow'. Πραμνείῳ οἴνῳ is 'with Pramnian wine', a named wine whose origin is not known. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 235.

sentences.t:
ἀνέμισγε δὲ σίτῳ
φάρμακα λύγρ’, ἵνα πάγχυ λαθοίατο πατρίδος αἴης.
sentences.tr:
anemisge de sitōi
pharmaka lygr’, hina panchy lathoiato patridos aiēs.
sentences.l:
and she mixed in with the grain
grievous drugs, so that quite they might forget their fatherland.
sentences.i: and she mixed grievous drugs in with the grain, so that they would forget their fatherland entirely.
sentences.n: ἀνέμισγε is the imperfect of ἀναμίσγω 'mix in', and σίτῳ is the dative of σῖτος 'grain, food'. φάρμακα λύγρ’ is 'grievous drugs', with the elided λυγρά and the adjective λυγρός 'grievous'. ἵνα with the optative λαθοίατο is 'so that they might forget', the optative ending -οίατο being the epic third plural. πάγχυ is 'altogether'. πατρίδος αἴης is 'of their fatherland', πατρίς with αἶα 'land', both in the genitive after λαθοίατο.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δῶκέν τε καὶ ἔκπιον, αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα
ῥάβδῳ πεπληγυῖα κατὰ συφεοῖσιν ἐέργνυ.
sentences.tr:
autar epei dōken te kai ekpion, autik’ epeita
rhabdōi peplēguia kata sypheoisin eergny.
sentences.l:
But when she gave it, and they drank it down, straightway then
with a wand having struck them, in the pigsties she shut them.
sentences.i: But when she had given it and they had drunk it down, at once she struck them with a wand and shut them up in the pigsties.
sentences.n: δῶκεν is the aorist 'gave' and ἔκπιον the aorist of ἐκπίνω 'drink up', unaugmented. αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα is 'straightway then'. ῥάβδῳ is the dative of ῥάβδος 'wand', and πεπληγυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of πλήσσω 'strike'. κατὰ … ἐέργνυ is 'shut in', the imperfect of the epic ἐέργνυμι (= ἔργνυμι, εἴργνυμι), and συφεοῖσιν is the dative plural of συφεός 'pigsty'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ συῶν μὲν ἔχον κεφαλὰς φωνήν τε τρίχας τε
καὶ δέμας, αὐτὰρ νοῦς ἦν ἔμπεδος, ὡς τὸ πάρος περ.
sentences.tr:
hoi de syōn men echon kephalas phōnēn te trichas te
kai demas, autar nous ēn empedos, hōs to paros per.
sentences.l:
and they of swine had the heads and voice and bristles
and shape, but the mind was steady, as before indeed.
sentences.i: They had the heads of swine, and the voices, bristles, and bodies, but their minds stayed steady, as before.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is 'and they', and συῶν is the genitive plural of σῦς 'swine', governed by the nouns it goes with. φωνήν is 'voice', τρίχας is 'hairs', here 'bristles', and δέμας is 'frame, body'. αὐτάρ marks the contrast, and νοῦς is 'mind'. ἔμπεδος is 'steady, unchanged', and ὡς τὸ πάρος περ is 'just as before'.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν κλαίοντες ἐέρχατο, τοῖσι δὲ Κίρκη
πάρ ῥ’ ἄκυλον βάλανόν τε βάλεν καρπόν τε κρανείης
ἔδμεναι, οἷα σύες χαμαιευνάδες αἰὲν ἔδουσιν.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men klaiontes eerchato, toisi de Kirkē
par rh’ akylon balanon te balen karpon te kraneiēs
edmenai, hoia syes chamaieunades aien edousin.
sentences.l:
So they, weeping, were shut in, and before them Circe
threw ilex-acorn and mast and the fruit of the cornel
to eat, such as swine that sleep on the ground always eat.
sentences.i: So they were penned in, weeping, and Circe threw before them ilex-acorn, mast, and the fruit of the cornel to eat, such as swine that sleep on the ground always eat.
sentences.n: ἐέρχατο is the pluperfect passive of ἔργω 'shut in', so 'they were (by then) shut in'. τοῖσι is 'for them', and πάρ ῥ’ … βάλεν is tmesis for παρέβαλεν 'threw beside, set before'. ἄκυλος is the edible acorn of the ilex, βάλανος 'acorn, mast', and κρανείη the cornel tree, whose fruit is a small red cherry. ἔδμεναι is the infinitive of ἔδω 'eat' in -μεναι. οἷα is 'such as', σύες χαμαιευνάδες is 'swine that sleep on the ground' (χαμαί 'on the ground', εὐνή 'bed'), and αἰέν is 'always'.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύλοχος δ’ αἶψ’ ἦλθε θοὴν ἐπὶ νῆα μέλαιναν
ἀγγελίην ἑτάρων ἐρέων καὶ ἀδευκέα πότμον.
sentences.tr:
Eurylochos d’ aips’ ēlthe thoēn epi nēa melainan
angeliēn hetarōn ereōn kai adeukea potmon.
sentences.l:
But Eurylochus quickly came to the swift black ship
to tell the news of his companions and their bitter doom.
sentences.i: But Eurylochus came quickly to the swift black ship, to bring news of his companions and their bitter doom.
sentences.n: ἦλθε is the aorist 'came', and θοὴν … νῆα μέλαιναν is 'the swift black ship'. ἐρέων is a future participle of ἐρέω 'tell', 'about to tell', and ἀγγελίην is 'news, message', with the genitive ἑτάρων 'of his companions'. ἀδευκέα is 'bitter', a rare old word whose precise sense is uncertain, and πότμον is 'doom'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι ἐκφάσθαι δύνατο ἔπος ἱέμενός περ,
κῆρ ἄχεϊ μεγάλῳ βεβολημένος·
sentences.tr:
oude ti ekphasthai dynato epos hiemenos per,
kēr acheï megalōi bebolēmenos·
sentences.l:
and not at all to speak out could he a word, eager though he was,
in heart with great grief struck;
sentences.i: He could not get a word out, eager as he was, his heart struck with great grief;
sentences.n: ἐκφάσθαι is the infinitive of ἐκφημί 'speak out', and δύνατο is the imperfect 'he was able', without augment. ἔπος is 'a word', and ἱέμενός περ is 'though eager'. κῆρ is 'in his heart', an accusative of respect, and βεβολημένος is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω 'struck', with ἄχεϊ μεγάλῳ 'with great grief'. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 247.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δακρυόφιν πίμπλαντο, γόον δ’ ὠίετο θυμός.
sentences.tr:
en de hoi osse
dakryophin pimplanto, goon d’ ōieto thymos.
sentences.l:
and in him the eyes
were filled with tears, and lamentation his heart expected.
sentences.i: his eyes filled with tears, and his heart foresaw lamentation.
sentences.n: ὄσσε is the dual 'the two eyes', and οἱ is the dative of the person affected, so ἐν δέ οἱ ὄσσε is 'and in him the eyes'. ἐν … πίμπλαντο is the imperfect passive of πίμπλημι 'fill', and δακρυόφιν is 'with tears', the ending -φιν being an old instrumental form. γόον is 'lament', and ὠίετο is the imperfect of ὀΐομαι 'expect, foresee'. θυμός is 'heart'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή μιν πάντες ἀγασσάμεθ’ ἐξερέοντες,
καὶ τότε τῶν ἄλλων ἑτάρων κατέλεξεν ὄλεθρον·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē min pantes agassameth’ exereontes,
kai tote tōn allōn hetarōn katelexen olethron·
sentences.l:
But when at last, him, all of us, in wonder, questioning,
then of the other companions he recounted the destruction:
sentences.i: But when at last we were all amazed at him and questioned him, then he recounted the destruction of the other companions:
sentences.n: ἀγασσάμεθ’ is the aorist of ἀγάομαι, a verb of strong feeling that can mean 'be amazed at' or 'resent'; here the sense is wonder at his state, and it is taken together with ἐξερέοντες 'asking out, questioning'. μιν is 'him'. καὶ τότε … κατέλεξεν is 'then he recounted', from καταλέγω, and ὄλεθρον is 'destruction'. The colon shows that Eurylochus's speech follows.

sentences.t: ἤιομεν, ὡς ἐκέλευες, ἀνὰ δρυμά, φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ·
sentences.tr: ēiomen, hōs ekeleues, ana dryma, phaidim’ Odysseu·
sentences.l: ‘We went, as you ordered, through the coppices, glorious Odysseus;
sentences.i: ‘We went through the coppices, as you ordered, glorious Odysseus;
sentences.n: ἤιομεν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go', 'we were going'. ὡς ἐκέλευες is 'as you ordered', and ἀνὰ δρυμά is 'up through the coppices'. φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ is 'glorious Odysseus', in the vocative. Line 251 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only if the ι and ο of ἤιομεν are run together into one short syllable (ἤ–ιο–μεν).

sentences.t:
εὕρομεν ἐν βήσσῃσι τετυγμένα δώματα καλὰ
ξεστοῖσιν λάεσσι, περισκέπτῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ.
sentences.tr:
heuromen en bēssēisi tetygmena dōmata kala
xestoisin laessi, periskeptōi eni chōrōi.
sentences.l:
we found in the glens well-wrought halls, fine,
of smoothed stones, in a place with a view all round.
sentences.i: We found in the glens fine halls, well-wrought, built of smoothed stone, in a place with a view all around.
sentences.n: Eurylochus now repeats what Odysseus told in lines 210–211, with εὕρομεν 'we found' for εὗρον and δώματα καλά 'fine halls' where the earlier line named Circe. τετυγμένα is 'well-wrought', ξεστοῖσιν λάεσσι is 'smoothed stones', and περισκέπτῳ ἐνὶ χώρῳ is 'in a place with a view all round'. The second line, 253, is the same as 211 and has the same English.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δέ τις μέγαν ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένη λίγ’ ἄειδεν,
ἢ θεὸς ἠὲ γυνή·
sentences.tr:
entha de tis megan histon epoichomenē lig’ aeiden,
ē theos ēe gynē·
sentences.l:
and there someone, at a great loom going to and fro, sang clearly,
either goddess or woman;
sentences.i: There someone, moving to and fro at a great loom, was singing in a clear voice, a goddess or a woman;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is 'there'. ἐποιχομένη μέγαν ἱστόν is 'going to and fro at a great loom', as before. λίγ’ ἄειδεν is 'sang clearly', λίγα being the neuter adverb of λιγύς 'clear-sounding', and ἄειδεν the uncontracted imperfect. ἢ θεὸς ἠὲ γυνή is the phrase of Polites's speech, 'either goddess or woman'. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τοὶ δὲ φθέγγοντο καλεῦντες.
sentences.tr: toi de phthengonto kaleuntes.
sentences.l: and they raised their voices, calling.
sentences.i: and they raised their voices and called.
sentences.n: The same words as the second half of line 229, with the same English: φθέγγοντο καλεῦντες is 'raised their voices, calling'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αἶψ’ ἐξελθοῦσα θύρας ὤιξε φαεινὰς
καὶ κάλει·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ aips’ exelthousa thyras ōixe phaeinas
kai kalei·
sentences.l:
And she at once, coming out, opened the shining doors
and called;
sentences.i: She came out at once, opened the shining doors, and called to them;
sentences.n: This is line 230 and the first half of 231 over again, with the same English.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἀιδρείῃσιν ἕποντο·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ hama pantes aidreiēisin heponto·
sentences.l: and they, all together, in their ignorance followed;
sentences.i: and in their ignorance they all followed together;
sentences.n: The second half of line 231 comes again with the same English.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ὑπέμεινα, ὀισάμενος δόλον εἶναι.
sentences.tr: autar egōn hypemeina, oisamenos dolon einai.
sentences.l: but I stayed behind, suspecting that it was a trick.
sentences.i: but I stayed behind, suspecting that it was a trick.
sentences.n: This is line 232 with αὐτάρ for δέ, ἐγών 'I' for Εὐρύλοχος, and ὑπέμεινα for ὑπέμεινεν. Eurylochus here says of himself what Odysseus has said of him. ὀισάμενος δόλον εἶναι is 'suspecting that it was a trick'.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἅμ’ ἀιστώθησαν ἀολλέες, οὐδέ τις αὐτῶν
ἐξεφάνη·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ham’ aistōthēsan aollees, oude tis autōn
exephanē·
sentences.l:
and they together vanished, all in a body, and not one of them
came into view;
sentences.i: They all vanished together, and not one of them came into view;
sentences.n: ἀιστώθησαν is the aorist passive of ἀιστόω 'make unseen', so 'they vanished'. ἀολλέες is 'all together, in a mass'. οὐδέ τις αὐτῶν is 'and not one of them', and ἐξεφάνη is the aorist passive of ἐκφαίνω, 'came into view'. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: δηρὸν δὲ καθήμενος ἐσκοπίαζον.
sentences.tr: dēron de kathēmenos eskopiazon.
sentences.l: and for a long time sitting I kept watch.’
sentences.i: and I sat watching for a long time.’
sentences.n: δηρόν is 'for a long time', and καθήμενος is 'sitting'. ἐσκοπίαζον is the imperfect of σκοπιάζω 'keep watch', from the same root as σκοπιή 'lookout'. The unit closes Eurylochus's report.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ περὶ μὲν ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
ὤμοιιν βαλόμην, μέγα χάλκεον, ἀμφὶ δὲ τόξα·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, autar egō peri men xiphos argyroēlon
ōmoiin balomēn, mega chalkeon, amphi de toxa·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, but I round, the silver-studded sword
on my shoulders slung, great, of bronze, and around me the bow;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and I slung my great bronze sword, silver-studded, about my shoulders, and my bow too;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'so he spoke', ἔφατ’ being ἔφατο without its final vowel. περί … βαλόμην is tmesis for 'I threw about myself', and the second ἀμφί … τόξα is the same with the bow. ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον is 'the silver-studded sword', ἀργυρόηλος being 'with silver nails', and μέγα χάλκεον is 'great, of bronze'. ὤμοιιν is the dual 'on both shoulders', and τόξα, plural, is used for a single bow. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἂψ ἠνώγεα αὐτὴν ὁδὸν ἡγήσασθαι.
sentences.tr: ton d’ aps ēnōgea autēn hodon hēgēsasthai.
sentences.l: and him back I ordered the very road to lead.
sentences.i: and I ordered him to lead me back the same way.
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', Eurylochus. ἠνώγεα is the pluperfect of ἀνώγω, with the sense of an imperfect, 'I ordered'. αὐτὴν ὁδόν is 'the very same road', and ἡγήσασθαι is the aorist infinitive 'to lead the way'. ἂψ is 'back'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἀμφοτέρῃσι λαβὼν ἐλλίσσετο γούνων
καί μ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ amphoterēisi labōn ellisseto gounōn
kai m’ olophyromenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
But he, with both hands taking my knees, entreated,
and me lamenting winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: But he took hold of my knees with both hands and begged me, and, lamenting, spoke winged words to me:
sentences.n: ὅ γε is 'he', Eurylochus. ἀμφοτέρῃσι is 'with both (hands)', the noun being understood, and γούνων is a genitive of what is grasped, 'by the knees', the posture of a suppliant; ἐλλίσσετο is the imperfect 'entreated'. καί μ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος is 'and me lamenting'. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula 'he spoke winged words'. The colon shows that his words follow.

sentences.t: μή μ’ ἄγε κεῖσ’ ἀέκοντα, διοτρεφές, ἀλλὰ λίπ’ αὐτοῦ.
sentences.tr: mē m’ age keis’ aekonta, diotrephes, alla lip’ autou.
sentences.l: ‘Do not lead me there, unwilling, Zeus-nurtured one, but leave me here.
sentences.i: ‘Do not lead me there unwilling, Zeus-nurtured one, but leave me here.
sentences.n: μή with the imperative ἄγε is 'do not lead'. κεῖσ’ is κεῖσε, 'to that place', and ἀέκοντα is 'unwilling'. διοτρεφές is the vocative of διοτρεφής 'Zeus-nurtured', a title of honour for a king. ἀλλά … λίπ’ αὐτοῦ is 'but leave me right here', λίπε the aorist imperative and αὐτοῦ 'on the spot'.

sentences.t:
οἶδα γάρ, ὡς οὔτ’ αὐτὸς ἐλεύσεαι οὔτε τιν’ ἄλλον
ἄξεις σῶν ἑτάρων.
sentences.tr:
oida gar, hōs out’ autos eleuseai oute tin’ allon
axeis sōn hetarōn.
sentences.l:
For I know that neither yourself will you come back nor any other
will you bring of your companions.
sentences.i: For I know that you will neither come back yourself nor bring back any other of your companions.
sentences.n: οἶδα γάρ, ὡς is 'for I know that'. οὔτ’ αὐτός … οὔτε τιν’ ἄλλον is 'neither yourself … nor any other', and ἐλεύσεαι is the future of ἔρχομαι 'you will come', with the epic ending -εαι for -ῃ. ἄξεις is the future 'you will bring', and σῶν ἑτάρων is 'of your companions'. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 268.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ ξὺν τοίσδεσι θᾶσσον
φεύγωμεν·
sentences.tr:
alla xyn toisdesi thasson
pheugōmen·
sentences.l:
But with these here more quickly
let us flee;
sentences.i: But let us flee quickly with these who are here;
sentences.n: ξύν is the old form of σύν 'with', and τοίσδεσι is a dative plural of ὅδε 'this one here', with the ending -εσσι; it means the men still beside the ship. φεύγωμεν is the subjunctive of φεύγω 'flee', used as an exhortation, and θᾶσσον is 'more quickly' (the second layer says simply 'quickly').

sentences.t: ἔτι γάρ κεν ἀλύξαιμεν κακὸν ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr: eti gar ken alyxaimen kakon ēmar.
sentences.l: for still we might escape the evil day.’
sentences.i: for we may still escape the evil day.’
sentences.n: ἔτι is 'still, yet', and κεν with the aorist optative ἀλύξαιμεν gives 'we might escape', from ἀλύσκω. κακὸν ἦμαρ is 'the evil day'. The unit closes Eurylochus's speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'so he spoke', and ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is 'answering, I addressed'; μιν is 'him' or 'her' alike. The English of this unit is the published wording of the same line at odyssey-017, where a woman was speaking, and it is wrong here: 'she' and 'her' should be 'he' and 'him', since Eurylochus has just spoken and Odysseus answers him (Εὐρύλοχ’ in the next line). It is kept character for character only because a repeated unit must match the published one. The colon shows that Odysseus's answer follows.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύλοχ’, ἦ τοι μὲν σὺ μέν’ αὐτοῦ τῷδ’ ἐνὶ χώρῳ
ἔσθων καὶ πίνων κοίλῃ παρὰ νηὶ μελαίνῃ·
sentences.tr:
Euryloch’, ē toi men sy men’ autou tōid’ eni chōrōi
esthōn kai pinōn koilēi para nēi melainēi·
sentences.l:
‘Eurylochus, truly, you indeed, remain here in this very place,
eating and drinking beside the hollow black ship;
sentences.i: ‘Eurylochus, as for you, stay here in this very place, eating and drinking beside the hollow black ship;
sentences.n: Εὐρύλοχ’ is the vocative. ἦ τοι μέν is 'truly, indeed', and σὺ μέν sets him against ἐγώ in the next line. μέν’ is μένε, 'stay' (the imperative of μένω), and αὐτοῦ τῷδ’ ἐνὶ χώρῳ is 'right here, in this very place'. ἔσθων καὶ πίνων is 'eating and drinking', and κοίλῃ παρὰ νηὶ μελαίνῃ is 'beside the hollow black ship'. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν εἶμι, κρατερὴ δέ μοι ἔπλετ’ ἀνάγκη.
sentences.tr: autar egōn eimi, kraterē de moi eplet’ anankē.
sentences.l: but I shall go, and strong upon me has come necessity.’
sentences.i: but I shall go, for a strong necessity has come upon me.’
sentences.n: ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ, and εἶμι is 'I shall go', the present form having a future sense. κρατερή is 'strong', δέ here gives the reason (so 'for' in the second layer), and ἔπλετ’ is ἔπλετο, an epic aorist of πέλομαι 'has come to be'. ἀνάγκη is 'necessity, compulsion', and μοι is 'to me, upon me'. The unit closes Odysseus's answer and the part.
